title: Digital Banking and the Future of Embedded Finance: How Will AI-Powered Fraud Detection and Algorithmic Credit Scoring in Cross-Border Rails Reshape Systemic Risk?
authors: Aggarwal, L.; Saravanan, T.; Loana, A.; Alisa; Shreshta
tldr: AI-powered fraud detection and algorithmic credit scoring are transforming global finance, but their convergence introduces systemic risks including model homogeneity, algorithmic herding, and data opacity requiring new macro-prudential governance frameworks.
problem_and_motivation: The global financial system is undergoing a structural shift where AI has moved from peripheral tools to the core of fraud detection, credit underwriting, and real-time payment verification. This rapid adoption creates tightly linked algorithmic environments where failures can cascade across jurisdictions, yet existing prudential frameworks are not equipped to manage synchronized algorithmic failures. The convergence of embedded finance, cross-border payments, and AI also introduces new vectors of systemic risk including model homogeneity, algorithmic herding, and opacity of cross-border data flows.
approach: Qualitative synthesis of industry reports, academic literature, and regulatory guidance on AI in global finance.
Case study analysis of Nubank, Tala, Nova Credit, and Mifundo demonstrating AI-driven financial innovation.
Examination of BIS Innovation Hub initiatives Project Aurora and Project Nexus for cross-border payment infrastructure.
Review of Graph Neural Networks for detecting money laundering networks in cross-border payment systems.
Analysis of algorithmic credit scoring using alternative data sources including mobile behavior and utility payments.
Evaluation of Privacy-Enhancing Technologies including federated learning for cross-border data sharing.
Assessment of systemic risks including algorithmic herding, model homogeneity, and concentration risk.
Framework analysis of macro-prudential regulatory recommendations from SUERF, Bank of England, and Financial Stability Board.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides a comprehensive synthesis of how AI is reshaping global financial infrastructure through fraud detection, credit scoring, and cross-border payment systems. It identifies emerging systemic risks including algorithmic herding, model homogeneity, and concentration risk that arise from widespread AI adoption in finance. By analyzing both public-sector initiatives such as BIS Project Aurora and Nexus alongside commercial applications from Tala, Nubank, Nova Credit, and Mifundo, the paper maps the current landscape of AI deployment in financial services. The paper argues that while AI is essential for managing high-velocity payment rails, it necessitates a new macro-prudential regulatory framework to prevent synchronized algorithmic failures across interconnected financial institutions.

limits: The paper is a qualitative review relying on secondary sources without original empirical data collection.
No quantitative modeling or simulation is performed to validate claimed systemic risk scenarios.
The analysis focuses primarily on developed markets and may not fully represent emerging economy conditions.
The proposed macro-prudential governance framework lacks specific implementation mechanisms or timelines.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All fourteen topic domains from the taxonomy were systematically scanned for relevance. The paper primarily covers AI applications in global finance including fraud detection, credit scoring, embedded finance, and cross-border payments, rather than personal budgeting or spending management. Domain 4.A was flagged as medium relevance because the paper describes the digital banking ecosystem that houses financial services relevant to personal finance contexts. Domain 4.B received medium relevance for identifying critical gaps in traditional rule-based fraud detection and conventional credit scoring systems. Domain 6.A was assigned medium relevance due to coverage of AI and ML predictive models applied to fraud detection and credit assessment. Domain 8.A received high relevance as AI-powered fraud detection using Graph Neural Networks is a central focus. Domain 8.B received high relevance for detailed discussion of GNN-based algorithms applied to cross-border transaction networks. Domain 10.A was assigned high relevance because the paper extensively covers data privacy risks, GDPR compliance, federated learning for privacy preservation, and cybersecurity threats. Domain 10.C received high relevance as cross-border credit data portability and Credit Passport technologies are analyzed in depth. Domains 1 through 3 (Filipino demographics, culturally specific practices, expense categorization), 5 (behavioral profiles), 7 (budgeting strategies), 9 (mobile-first design), 11 (engagement dynamics), 12 (evaluation frameworks), 13 (savings and debt management), and 14 (synthetic data and model serving) were all considered and rejected as the paper does not address personal finance management, budgeting, or the specific technical concerns of those domains. The paper's macro-level focus on global financial infrastructure places it at the periphery of the personal finance systems taxonomy.
